paras: The lynching of Ross Hollis was the hanging of Ross Hollis, a Black corporal of the Twenty-fifth United States Infantry at Fort Meade, by a mob at Sturgis, Dakota Territory, in late August 1885. Hollis was accused of shooting Dr. H. P. Lynch, a Sturgis physician, and after a coroner's jury returned a verdict against him he was taken from the town calaboose and hanged. White papers carried the story as swift punishment for an "assassination," and a second dispatch reported that armed Black soldiers had threatened to burn the town.

According to the Deadwood wire report, Hollis had earlier beaten "a colored woman," breaking three of her ribs, and after Lynch, who treated her, testified before the grand jury and Hollis was indicted, Hollis threatened to kill the doctor. A special from Sturgis to the St. Paul Pioneer Press told it differently, saying that Lynch, called to attend "a woman of the town" whom Hollis had injured, denounced Hollis and threatened to file a criminal complaint. That special added jealousy as a motive, saying Hollis believed Lynch "too attentive" to the woman.

The wire report said that on Monday night Hollis deserted the fort, changed his clothes, went to Sturgis and fired at Lynch through the window of his office. The Sturgis special and the National Tribune instead placed the shooting on Saturday evening; the special said Hollis left his guard post, borrowed a friend's clothes and revolver, and shot Lynch in his store as he sat reading.

Hollis was arrested, and wire reports said he confessed when confronted with "proofs of his guilt." The Sturgis special mentioned no confession but said a coroner's inquest returned a verdict "criminating" Hollis, after which the populace became "greatly excited." At 10:30 in the evening the crowd went to the calaboose, overpowered the two guards, took Hollis to a secluded spot behind the Catholic church and hanged him. Other versions said he was "hanged by the citizens" or taken "just outside of town" about midnight.

Lynch, said to be 53 years old and a resident of the Hills since 1876, was buried with Masonic honors. A Deadwood dispatch dated August 28 reported that armed Black soldiers of the Twenty-fifth Infantry went to Sturgis threatening to burn it, until Gen. Sturgis, commanding at Fort Meade, sent a Seventh Cavalry patrol that returned "the disaffected men" to the post. The Sturgis special described only rumors of such a plan, which led residents to arm themselves, and said soldiers from the fort stayed in town overnight without any demonstration.
No report of an inquest into Hollis's death or of arrests among the mob appears in the coverage.

The Deadwood wire story of August 27 ran that day and the next from Washington and Bismarck to Memphis, Waco and Wheeling. Its headlines leaned toward the mob: the Washington Critic printed "Quick Retribution," the Memphis paper "A Dastardly Assassination and Swift Punishment," the Waco paper "Murder, Confession and Murder," and the Savannah Morning News "Disgraced His Uniform."

The follow-up dispatch about the soldiers ran on August 28 and 29 under headlines such as "Colored Soldiers on the Warpath" and "Hollis' Friends Threaten Vengeance." The New-York Tribune headed it "The Lynching of the Colored Soldier," and the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner reprinted it as late as September 9. The fuller Sturgis special appeared in the Omaha Daily Bee on August 29 and was reprinted in the New Ulm Weekly Review and the Bad Lands Cow Boy in early September.

The McCook Tribune paired the case with a Texas lynching under "Lynchers of Dakota and Texas Get in Their Work," calling Hollis "a negro." None of the white reports questioned Hollis's guilt or criticized the lynchers, and no Black-press account of the lynching was found.

The dates are uncertain: the wire put the lynching on Tuesday night, August 25, but other printings of it said "Last night" under an August 27 dateline, as did the Sturgis special, the most local account and the only one to report the inquest; the Rock Island Argus said Wednesday night. Accounts also differ on the day of the shooting (Monday or Saturday), on whether Hollis confessed, and on whether armed soldiers actually entered Sturgis.

bases: A mob or 'the populace' took Hollis, a Black soldier accused of murder, from the Sturgis calaboose and hanged him (A1, A13, A20).

Hollis was hanged by 'a mob' or the townspeople after being taken from custody past two guards, with no lawful authority, in retaliation for the killing of Dr. Lynch of which he was accused (A1, A13, A9).

Three independently sourced dispatches (the Deadwood wire, the Pioneer Press special from Sturgis, and a Rapid City dispatch) agree that Hollis was accused of killing Lynch and was hanged by a mob, though they differ on dates and details (A1, A13, A20).

accounts.label: Deadwood wire (Aug. 27)
accounts.gist: Hollis shot Lynch through his office window Monday night in revenge for Lynch's grand-jury testimony, was arrested, confessed, and was seized and hanged by a mob Tuesday night.

accounts.label: Sturgis special to the Pioneer Press
accounts.gist: Hollis shot Lynch in his store Saturday evening, moved by Lynch's threat of a complaint and by jealousy; after a coroner's verdict against him, the excited populace overpowered two guards at the calaboose and hanged him behind the Catholic church at 10:30.

accounts.label: Rapid City dispatch
accounts.gist: Lynch was shot Wednesday night by an unknown person; suspicion fell on Hollis, who was arrested, confessed, and was lynched just outside town about midnight.

accounts.label: Deadwood dispatch (Aug. 28)
accounts.gist: Armed Black soldiers of the 25th Infantry went to Sturgis threatening to burn it and were captured and returned to the post by a 7th Cavalry patrol after Lynch's burial.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Quick Retribution. A Murderer Lynched' and 'A Dastardly Assassination and Swift Punishment' presented the lynching as deserved.
Wire reprints carried the Deadwood account under 'Corporal Hollis Lynched', 'Murder, Confession and Murder', 'Disgraced His Uniform' and 'A Soldier Lynched'.
The threat-to-burn dispatch ran as 'Colored Soldiers on the Warpath' and 'Hollis' Friends Threaten Vengeance', calling Hollis 'the colored soldier assassin'.
The McCook Tribune paired the case with a Texas lynching as 'Lynchers of Dakota and Texas Get in Their Work', calling Hollis 'a negro' and the woman 'a wench'.

Two deaths in the episode: Dr. Lynch (shot; race not stated) and Hollis (lynched); no one is reported killed in the soldiers' threatened march
